think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 66-year-old male recently initiated on quadruple antimycobacterial therapy for pulmonary granulomatous opacities suddenly develops acute near-syncope, diaphoresis, nausea, and involuntary conjugate upward and lateral gaze deviation. This presentation closely mimics acute anaphylaxis or an acute cerebrovascular event, obscuring an acute drug-induced dystonic reaction (oculogyric crisis) precipitated by anti-tuberculosis pharmacotherapy.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following emergency triage, physical and neurological examination, and baseline cardiorespiratory and metabolic evaluations, strictly prior to the administration and therapeutic response of intravenous diphenhydramine and send-out mycobacterial cultures.
3. Differential Distinctions: Anaphylactoid drug reaction typically features urticaria, angioedema, hypotension, and respiratory distress, whereas this patient experienced intact consciousness with acute involuntary ocular dystonia. Trauma can precipitate acute cranial nerve or ocular deviation, but was absent in this patient.
case_prompt:
A 66-year-old Indian male presented to the emergency department after the sudden onset of near-syncope, nausea, diaphoresis, light-headedness, and a wide-staring gaze with upward and lateral deviation of both eyes. The symptoms began abruptly 30 minutes after ingesting newly prescribed daily medications comprising rifampicin 600 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, ethambutol 1.6 g, pyrazinamide 1.75 g, and pyridoxine 10 mg. He had been initiated on this combination antimicrobial regimen following sequential chest radiographs that revealed increased nodular opacities in the left upper zone, suggestive of granulomata, accompanied by a small calcified pleural plaque. He had no recent history of trauma.

On physical examination upon arrival, his vital signs were stable. He was conscious and alert to his surroundings but felt physically blocked, unable to respond with purposeful voluntary movements or speech, and noted generalized weakness and abdominal discomfort. General physical examination was unremarkable, and a focused neurological examination revealed no conclusive focal motor or sensory deficits outside of the sustained conjugate ocular deviation. Initial triage evaluations—including a complete blood count, liver function tests, thyroid function tests, urine toxicology drug screen, cardiac troponin I, an electrocardiogram, and a two-dimensional echocardiogram—were normal or non-diagnostic.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the hyperacute onset of diaphoresis, light-headedness, nausea, and near-syncope within 30 minutes of ingesting a newly prescribed medication regimen. However, there were no manifestations of hemodynamic collapse, bronchospasm, urticaria, or angioedema, and further evaluation revealed preserved awareness with isolated dystonic motor blockage.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient was referred, initially, to the Department of Rheumatology, Allergy and Immunology based on the suspicion of a reaction to RHEZ. A diagnosis of anaphylaxis-like and possibly idiosyncratic reaction to rifampicin was made. ... On further questioning by the primary team, the patient reported that while he was aware of his surroundings and was able to hear conversations around him, he felt "physical blocked" in that he was unable to respond with purposeful voluntary movements or speech

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because sudden conjugate gaze deviation or oculogyric dystonia may occur secondary to acute brainstem or cranial injury, but excluded by history and physical examination.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Another possible cause of OGC would include trauma. However, the patient did not suffer from any trauma recently.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The dramatic and complete resolution of symptoms following intravenous diphenhydramine, alongside the characteristic conjugate eye deviation and temporal link to antimycobacterial ingestion, confirmed an acute oculogyric crisis induced by standard quadruple anti-tuberculosis therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: These symptoms resolved on the administration of diphenhydramine 25 mg intravenously at the Emergency Department. ... However, the diagnosis was subsequently changed to OGC based on the more complete history recorded.

editor_comments: The patient developed an acute oculogyric crisis (OGC) secondary to first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy (RHEZ). This case highlights the importance of distinguishing medication-induced extrapyramidal and dystonic side effects from systemic anaphylactoid or cerebrovascular events in patients undergoing treatment for tuberculosis.
